tickets.title: Apps can be granted the MANAGE_APPS permission, allowing them to escalate beyond their initial permission scope
tickets.body:
Previously there was only partial protection against granting app a MANAGE_APPS permission.

Apps should not have one, because in such case it can leak of the initial permission scope.

This PR targets missing spots: commands, human/admin mutations as well

No port - this *may* be a breaking change. Users that have such apps in existing env, will not be able to reinstall them, hence I introduce it to 3.24

Migration guide https://github.com/saleor/saleor-docs/pull/1785

- [x] Migration - in 3.24 remove permission from apps
- [x] Raise error when trying to issue token of such an app
tickets.body_sanitized:
Apps must never hold the MANAGE_APPS permission. If an app is granted MANAGE_APPS, it can be used to leak/escalate beyond the app's initial permission scope, since MANAGE_APPS would let it manage (and thus widen the permissions of) apps.

Currently there is only partial protection against granting an app the MANAGE_APPS permission. Some code paths still allow it to be assigned. The gaps span multiple entry points, including commands and human/admin (staff) mutations.

Expected behavior: across all paths where app permissions can be set or modified (commands and human/admin mutations alike), it should not be possible to grant an app the MANAGE_APPS permission.

Note: This is potentially a breaking change. Users who currently have apps with MANAGE_APPS in an existing environment will no longer be able to reinstall those apps.

tickets.title: fix: move all risky usages of set_password()
tickets.body:
This moves all insecure usages of `set_password()` outside of tests which could otherwise be accidentally used for production thus allowing users to bypass password requirements due to lack of validation.

This also prefixes the functions' names with `dangerously_[...]` to make it clear that these functions shouldn't be used (or rather: be used carefully).

This fixes Semgrep errors like this one:

    saleor/account/utils.py
    ❯❱ python.django.security.audit.unvalidated-password.unvalidated-password
          ❰❰ Blocking ❱❱
          The password on 'user' is being set without validating the password. Call
          django.contrib.auth.password_validation.validate_password() with validation functions before setting
          the password. See https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.0/topics/auth/passwords/ for more information.
          Details: https://sg.run/OPBL

           ▶▶┆ Autofix ▶ if django.contrib.auth.password_validation.validate_password(credentials["password"],
              user=user): user.set_password(credentials["password"])
          138┆ user.set_password(credentials["password"])

In the future we might also want to just fully remove these hardcoded test passwords in favor of random passwords. Likewise for populatedb command.

This also removes support for custom `User` models in `./manage.py createsuperuser` command as custom models are currently not supported by our GraphQL mutations thus no one likely is using custom models. This simplifies the changes in this PR as it would be slightly trickier.

tickets.body_sanitized:
During address validation, fields that exist on the original address but are not part of the country's standard address format are cleared (dropped). This happens by default, and there is currently no way to keep those extra fields when validating an address.

In some cases, the extra data carried on an address is meaningful and should survive validation rather than being discarded. Today there is no option to retain it — once an address is validated, any field outside the target country's expected format is lost.

Provide a way for operators to opt into preserving these additional fields so that they are not removed during address validation. The existing default behavior (clearing the extra fields) must remain unchanged for anyone who does not opt in.

There is no top-level GraphQL query for listing payment transactions, and existing transaction access is too limited.

Requirements:

1. Provide a way to query transactions across the API, with access scoped by permission:
   - Apps with `MANAGE_ORDERS` can see all transactions.
   - Apps with only `HANDLE_PAYMENTS` can see only the transactions they created.
   - Staff users can see transactions belonging to orders/checkouts in channels they have access to.

2. The existing `transaction` query is too restrictive: users with the `manage_orders` permission cannot fetch a transaction. They should be permitted to do so.

3. Order transactions cannot currently be filtered by PSP reference. Filtering order transactions by PSP reference should be supported.

tickets.body_sanitized:
Addresses are shared (the same address instance is referenced) between `Checkout` and `Order` objects. When an order is created from a checkout via the `OrderFromCheckout` mutation, the resulting `Order` ends up pointing at the same address records as the originating `Checkout` rather than having its own independent copies.

This shared-instance relationship is a problem because:
- When the checkout is not removed after the order is created, the `Checkout` and the resulting `Order` continue to reference the same address records, so changes to one are reflected in the other.
- More broadly, `Checkout` and `Order` objects should not share address instances at all.

Expected behavior: an `Order` created from a `Checkout` should have its own independent address records, so that subsequent modifications to the checkout's addresses (or the order's) do not affect the other object.

tickets.title: AppExtension configuration still stored in legacy `target`/`http_target_method` fields instead of the new `settings` field
tickets.body:
Replaces #18518

- [x] Fix tests for migration
- [x] Benchmark migration

## Summary

This PR migrates AppExtension data from the old `target` and `http_target_method` fields to the new `settings` JSON field format. The migration is performed asynchronously using a Celery task to avoid blocking deployments.

## Changes

- **Database Migration**: Added migration `0035_app_extensions_mount_target_settings_reshape.py` that triggers a post-migrate signal to enqueue the data migration task
- **Celery Task**: Implemented `fill_app_extension_settings_task` that migrates data in batches of 100 records
- **Data Migration Logic**:
  - For `WIDGET` target: moves `http_target_method` to `settings.widgetTarget.method`
  - For `NEW_TAB` target: moves `http_target_method` to `settings.newTabTarget.method`
  - Preserves existing non-empty settings (only fills empty settings objects)
  - Processes records in batches for performance
- **Model Changes**: Removed enum constraints from `mount` and `target` fields to allow more flexibility
- **Tests**: Added comprehensive test coverage for the migration task

## Migration Strategy

The migration uses a post-migrate signal to enqueue a Celery task, ensuring:
- Non-blocking deployment process
- Batch processing for better performance
- Safe migration that preserves existing settings
- Only migrates AppExtension records with empty settings

## Test Plan

- [x] Migration task implemented with Celery
- [x] Tests cover all scenarios (widget, new_tab, skip filled settings)
- [ ] Verify migration runs successfully on staging
tickets.body_sanitized:
AppExtension configuration data is stored in the legacy `target` and `http_target_method` fields, but it should live in the new `settings` JSON field format. Existing AppExtension records need to have their data moved into the `settings` field.

Requirements for the resulting data:
- Existing non-empty `settings` values must be preserved (not overwritten).
- For AppExtensions whose target is WIDGET or NEW_TAB, the `http_target_method` value must be mapped into the corresponding shape within `settings`.

tickets.title: Obsolete validation code remains for removed AppExtension fields (mount, target, options)
tickets.body:
## Summary
Removes obsolete validation code for deprecated AppExtension fields that were removed in #18571. This cleanup removes:
- Manifest validation functions for `mount`, `target`, and `options` fields
- Pydantic validators for extension options (newTabTarget, widgetTarget)
- URL validation logic specific to different target types
- 153 lines of tests for the deleted validation functions

Additionally marks the legacy enums (`AppExtensionMount`, `AppExtensionTarget`, `AppExtensionHttpMethod`) as deprecated by renaming them to `Deprecated*` variants, signaling their obsolescence while maintaining backward compatibility in the database layer.

## Changes

### Manifest Validations (`manifest_validations.py`)
- Removed `_clean_extension_url_with_only_path` - validated relative URLs for different targets
- Simplified `_clean_extension_url` - now only validates app URL, removed target-specific logic
- Removed validation for POST method extensions with hostname matching
- Removed imports: `PydanticValidationError`, `AppExtensionMount`, `AppExtensionTarget`
- Added `DEFAULT_APP_TARGET` constant for fallback handling

### Validators (`validators.py`)
- Removed `NewTabTargetOptions` Pydantic model
- Removed `WidgetTargetOptions` Pydantic model
- Removed `AppExtensionOptions` Pydantic model with mutual exclusivity validation
- Removed `validate_POST_or_GET_http_method` validator
- Removed 60 lines of validation code

The legacy enums are now marked as deprecated (via naming convention) to signal that while they remain in the database layer for backward compatibility, they should not be used in new code.
tickets.body_sanitized: The AppExtension fields `mount`, `target`, and `options` have been removed, but validation code for these deprecated fields still exists. This now-obsolete validation logic is dead code and should be cleaned up.
